plan.why: The Lilly release went out on 29 Sep and pill searches are growing. A framework for reading indirect comparisons stands out from finance-media headlines and gets saved. | fact-check: Confirmed the Lilly press release (EASD 2026, Milan): Foundayo 17.2 mg vs oral semaglutide 25 mg in adults with T2D, ACHIEVE-3 vs PIONEER PLUS, indirect treatment comparison. The release page timed out, so re-verify the ~1.5-point weight and ~0.3-point A1C differences and the 52-week timepoint before use. The Novo-side analysis is published: 'Oral Semaglutide 25 mg Versus Orforglipron 36 mg in Obesity: A Population-Adjusted Indirect Treatment Comparison' (PubMed 42225305; OASIS 4 vs ATTAIN-1). It favoured oral semaglutide by about 3 percentage points in weight. Label it Novo-funded, obesity population, different orforglipron dose. Regulatory caution: FDA approved Foundayo in April 2026 for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition. Sources suggest a US type 2 diabetes indication was not approved as of the search (Lilly planned to file), and the EU is still under review. So the comparison is in a population the US label may not cover. The slides must not imply it's approved for T2D, and each regional statement must be checked against the FDA label and EMA pages. Doses may appear only as trial identifiers.

package.title: GLP-1 Pill vs GLP-1 Pill: How to Read the New Comparisons

social.facebook_caption:
You may have seen two very different headlines this year: one (from Lilly, out this week at EASD 2026) says orforglipron beats oral semaglutide, and one (from Novo-funded research reported back in April 2026) says oral semaglutide wins. Both are talking about the same two pills — so what's going on?

Neither headline comes from a true head-to-head trial at the higher doses. Lilly's own indirect comparison, in adults with type 2 diabetes, estimated orforglipron 17.2 mg ahead at 52 weeks (1.5 percentage points more weight loss, 0.3 points more A1C lowering) versus oral semaglutide 25 mg, a dose not US-approved for type 2 diabetes. Separately, the Novo-funded analysis, in adults with overweight or obesity and no diabetes, estimated oral semaglutide 25 mg about 3 percentage points ahead on weight loss versus orforglipron's top dose. Different companies, different people studied, different trials — so naturally, different answers.

The honest takeaway: these are statistical estimates, not races.

factcheck.summary:
The carousel is accurate and safe to publish. I checked all six sources and they exist and say what the slides claim.

- **Lilly analysis (29 Sep 2026, EASD):** At 52 weeks, orforglipron 17.2 mg showed 1.5 percentage points more weight loss and 0.3 points more A1C lowering than oral semaglutide 25 mg, in adults with type 2 diabetes. It used ACHIEVE-3 and PIONEER PLUS. The release also says the 25 mg dose isn't US-approved for type 2 diabetes.
- **Novo analysis:** This is the Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism paper (2026, Novo-funded, PMID 42225305). It used OASIS 4 and ATTAIN-1 in adults with overweight or obesity and no diabetes. The weight-loss gap was 3.2 points (95% CI 0.4 to 5.9) in the main analysis and 3.0 points in the second.
- **ACHIEVE-3 (The Lancet 2026):** Orforglipron 12 mg and 36 mg vs oral semaglutide 7 mg and 14 mg over 52 weeks, as the slide says.
- **US label (DailyMed):** Approved for weight management only.
- **UK (MHRA, 10 Aug 2026):** Authorised for weight management and for type 2 diabetes.

The framing is right throughout: comparisons are called indirect, company funding is disclosed, and the populations are named correctly. The prescriber line is present and exact.

There are three minor wording fixes: a 'capsule' wording the source doesn't support, a limitation that is paraphrased more strongly than the source, and a US-approval line that could be misread.

issues.claim: orforglipron's 36 mg trial capsule is considered equivalent to the 17.2 mg tablet
issues.problem: Healio, the cited source, calls the trial dose '36 mg tablets' that are equivalent to FDA-approved doses up to 17.2 mg. It doesn't say 'capsule', so that word isn't backed by the cited source.
issues.fix: Different companies, people, trials and timepoints (same top doses: orforglipron's 36 mg trial dose is considered equivalent to the approved 17.2 mg tablet): each analysis answers a different question. Sources: Lilly press release, 29 Sep 2026; PubMed 42225305; Healio.

issues.claim: the Novo paper's authors note cross-trial comparisons limit interpretation
issues.problem: This is a paraphrase attributed to the authors. The abstract only says the results apply 'in the absence of head-to-head clinical trials' and that the analysis adjusted for baseline differences. It's Healio that describes the limits of trial-design differences. The wording is slightly stronger than what the source says.
issues.fix: Indirect estimates carry more uncertainty than a head-to-head trial; the Novo paper notes its results come in the absence of head-to-head trials

issues.claim: Type 2 diabetes isn't an approved US use yet.
issues.problem: This is correct: there's no US approval for blood-sugar control. But the US weight-management label does include adults who have type 2 diabetes (its Trial 2 enrolled them), so some readers may think people with type 2 diabetes can't be prescribed it for weight.
issues.fix: Treating type 2 diabetes (blood-sugar control) isn't an approved US use yet.
